name: Shear Modulus from E and Poisson's Ratio
description: Calculates the shear modulus of an isotropic material from its Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio, as Young's modulus divided by twice one plus Poisson's ratio. It links the three elastic constants of an isotropic solid.
notes: Valid only for isotropic materials; Poisson's ratio must lie between -1 and 0.5. Young's modulus and the result share the same pressure unit (pascals here).

name: Bulk Modulus from E and Poisson's Ratio
description: Calculates the bulk modulus of an isotropic material from its Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio, as Young's modulus divided by three times one minus twice Poisson's ratio. The bulk modulus measures resistance to uniform compression.
notes: Valid for isotropic materials only. As Poisson's ratio approaches 0.5 the denominator tends to zero and bulk modulus diverges, describing an incompressible material.

name: Young's Modulus from Bulk and Shear Modulus
description: Calculates Young's modulus of an isotropic material from its bulk and shear moduli, as nine times bulk times shear divided by three times bulk plus shear. It converts the volumetric and shear elastic constants into the tensile modulus.
notes: Valid for isotropic materials only. All three moduli share the same pressure unit (pascals here); the result is the axial stiffness in tension or compression.

name: Poisson's Ratio from Bulk and Shear Modulus
description: Calculates Poisson's ratio of an isotropic material from its bulk and shear moduli, as three times bulk minus twice shear divided by twice three times bulk plus shear. Poisson's ratio is the negative ratio of transverse to axial strain.
notes: Valid for isotropic materials only; the dimensionless result should fall between -1 and 0.5. Both moduli must share the same pressure unit for the ratio to be correct.

name: Hall-Petch Relation (Yield Strength)
description: Gives the yield strength of a polycrystalline metal by the Hall-Petch relation, as a friction stress plus a strengthening coefficient divided by the square root of the grain diameter. Finer grains raise yield strength.
notes: Grain diameter must be in metres, matching the coefficient's units of Pa times metre to the half power. The relation breaks down at nanoscale grain sizes where inverse Hall-Petch behaviour can appear.

name: Arrhenius Diffusion Coefficient
description: Calculates the temperature-dependent diffusion coefficient from the Arrhenius law, as the pre-exponential factor times the exponential of minus the activation energy over the gas constant times absolute temperature. Diffusion rises steeply with temperature.
notes: Temperature must be in kelvin and activation energy per mole to match the gas constant. The exponential makes diffusion extremely sensitive to temperature, so small temperature errors matter.

name: Diffusion Length
description: Gives the characteristic diffusion length, the distance a species spreads by diffusion in a given time, as the square root of the diffusion coefficient times the time. It sets the scale of concentration profiles in heat treatment and doping.
notes: Diffusion coefficient and time must be in consistent SI units (m squared per second and seconds). This gives the order-of-magnitude penetration depth, not a sharp boundary.

name: Mode I Stress Intensity Factor
description: Calculates the Mode I (opening) stress intensity factor at a crack tip, as a geometry factor times the applied stress times the square root of pi times the crack length. It quantifies the stress field driving crack growth.
notes: Crack length must be in metres; result units are Pa times metre to the half power. The geometry factor depends on crack and specimen shape; fracture occurs when this reaches the fracture toughness.

name: Critical Crack Length
description: Gives the critical crack length at which fast fracture occurs, as one over pi times the square of the fracture toughness divided by the geometry factor times the applied stress. Cracks longer than this grow unstably at the given stress.
notes: Result is in metres. It is the inverse of the stress intensity relation, so higher toughness allows longer tolerable cracks while higher stress shortens them sharply.

name: Griffith Fracture Stress
description: Gives the Griffith fracture stress for a brittle material, as the square root of twice Young's modulus times surface energy divided by pi times the crack half-length. It is the stress at which an existing crack propagates in an ideally brittle solid.
notes: Applies to brittle materials where plastic work is negligible; here the crack length is the half-length. Surface energy is per unit area, and all quantities use SI units.

name: Plastic Zone Size (Plane Stress)
description: Estimates the size of the plastic zone at a crack tip under plane stress, as one over two pi times the square of the stress intensity factor divided by the yield strength. It indicates the extent of yielding ahead of the crack.
notes: This is the plane-stress estimate; the plane-strain zone is about three times smaller. Linear elastic fracture mechanics is valid only when this zone is small compared with crack and specimen dimensions.

name: Vickers Hardness Number
description: Calculates the Vickers hardness number from a diamond pyramid indentation, as 1.8544 times the test load divided by the square of the mean diagonal length. It measures a material's resistance to indentation.
notes: Load is in kilogram-force and diagonal in millimetres, giving hardness in kgf per mm squared. The 1.8544 constant embeds the 136-degree indenter geometry; use the average of the two diagonals.

name: Brinell Hardness Number
description: Calculates the Brinell hardness number from a ball indentation, as twice the test load divided by pi times the ball diameter times the diameter minus the square root of ball diameter squared minus indentation diameter squared. It divides load by the curved indent area.
notes: Ball and indentation diameters are in millimetres and load in kilogram-force, giving kgf per mm squared. Indentation diameter must be smaller than the ball diameter or the root becomes invalid.

name: Schmid Factor
description: Computes the Schmid factor, the geometric factor relating applied axial stress to the resolved shear stress on a slip system, as the cosine of the angle to the slip-plane normal times the cosine of the angle to the slip direction.
notes: Both angles must be in radians. The factor ranges from 0 to 0.5; its maximum of 0.5 occurs when both angles are 45 degrees, giving the most favourably oriented slip system.

name: Resolved Shear Stress (Schmid's Law)
description: Gives the resolved shear stress on a slip system by Schmid's law, as the applied stress times the cosine of the angle to the slip-plane normal times the cosine of the angle to the slip direction. Slip begins when this reaches the critical resolved shear stress.
notes: Both angles must be in radians and the applied stress is uniaxial. The product of cosines is the Schmid factor; the resolved shear stress is always less than or equal to the applied stress.

name: Interplanar Spacing (Cubic Crystal)
description: Gives the spacing between adjacent lattice planes in a cubic crystal, as the lattice parameter divided by the square root of the sum of the squared Miller indices h, k and l. This spacing sets the diffraction angles in X-ray analysis.
notes: Valid only for cubic crystal systems. Miller indices are integers; larger index planes are more closely spaced. Lattice parameter and result share length units.

name: Theoretical Density of Crystal
description: Calculates the theoretical density of a crystal from its structure, as the number of atoms per unit cell times the atomic weight divided by the cell volume (lattice parameter cubed) times Avogadro's number. It predicts density from crystallography alone.
notes: Assumes a cubic cell (volume is the lattice parameter cubed) and a perfect defect-free lattice. Atomic weight is per mole; keep lattice parameter in metres for a kg per m cubed result.

name: Lattice Parameter (FCC from Atomic Radius)
description: Gives the lattice parameter (cube edge length) of a face-centred cubic crystal from the atomic radius, as two times the square root of two times the radius. It follows from atoms touching along the face diagonal.
notes: Applies specifically to the FCC structure, where atoms contact along the face diagonal. Radius and result share length units; use the correct geometry factor for other structures.

name: Lattice Parameter (BCC from Atomic Radius)
description: Gives the lattice parameter (cube edge length) of a body-centred cubic crystal from the atomic radius, as four times the radius divided by the square root of three. It follows from atoms touching along the body diagonal.
notes: Applies specifically to the BCC structure, where atoms contact along the body diagonal. Radius and result share length units; the FCC relation differs and must not be substituted.

name: Fourier Heat Conduction Rate
description: Gives the steady one-dimensional heat conduction rate through a slab by Fourier's law, as thermal conductivity times cross-section area times the temperature difference divided by the thickness. It is the heat power flowing across the wall.
notes: Assumes steady state, one-dimensional conduction and constant conductivity. Temperature difference can be in kelvin or degrees Celsius since only the difference matters; thickness is along the heat flow.

name: Wiedemann-Franz Thermal Conductivity
description: Estimates the electronic thermal conductivity of a metal from the Wiedemann-Franz law, as the Lorenz number times the electrical conductivity times the absolute temperature. It links a metal's heat and charge transport by electrons.
notes: Temperature must be in kelvin. It captures only the electronic contribution, so it underestimates conductivity where phonons matter, and holds best at high or very low temperatures.

name: Electrical Resistivity Temperature Dependence
description: Gives the electrical resistivity of a metal at a changed temperature, as the reference resistivity times one plus the temperature coefficient times the temperature change. It captures the near-linear rise of metal resistivity with temperature.
notes: The linear model holds over moderate temperature ranges near the reference; it fails at very low temperatures and far from the reference. Temperature change and coefficient must use matching kelvin-based units.

name: Electrical Conductivity (Carrier Model)
description: Calculates the electrical conductivity of a material from its charge carriers, as the carrier density times the elementary charge times the carrier mobility. It expresses conductivity in terms of how many carriers there are and how easily they move.
notes: Assumes a single carrier type; for semiconductors with both electrons and holes, sum each carrier's contribution. Use SI units throughout for a result in siemens per metre.

name: Matthiessen's Rule (Total Resistivity)
description: Gives the total electrical resistivity of a metal by Matthiessen's rule, as the sum of the thermal (phonon) resistivity and the impurity resistivity. It treats the independent scattering mechanisms as simply additive.
notes: The rule assumes scattering sources are independent, which is approximate. The impurity term is temperature-independent while the thermal term rises with temperature; both share the same unit.

name: Norton Power-Law Creep Rate
description: Gives the steady-state creep strain rate by Norton's power law, as a material constant times the stress raised to the stress exponent times the exponential of minus the activation energy over the gas constant times temperature. It combines stress and thermal effects on creep.
notes: Temperature must be in kelvin and activation energy per mole. The material constant's units depend on the stress exponent and the stress unit used, so stress here (MPa) must match how the constant was fitted.

name: Larson-Miller Parameter
description: Computes the Larson-Miller parameter used to correlate creep rupture data, as the absolute temperature times the sum of a material constant and the base-10 logarithm of the rupture time. It combines time and temperature into one value for extrapolating creep life.
notes: Temperature must be in kelvin and rupture time in hours (log base 10). The material constant is typically around 20 for many alloys but should be fitted to the specific material.

name: Linear Thermal Expansion (Elongation)
description: Calculates how much a solid rod lengthens when heated. The change in length equals the original length times the linear expansion coefficient times the temperature change, giving the absolute elongation in metres.
notes: Result is the change in length, not the final length; add it to L0 for the new length. The coefficient alpha is roughly constant only over moderate temperature ranges.

name: Volumetric Thermal Expansion
description: Estimates the volume increase of a solid on heating. The volume change equals three times the linear expansion coefficient times the original volume times the temperature change, since volumetric expansion is about three times the linear value for isotropic materials.
notes: The factor 3 assumes an isotropic material and small expansion; alpha here is the linear coefficient, not the volumetric one. Result is the change in volume, not the final volume.

name: Critical Nucleus Radius (Homogeneous Nucleation)
description: Gives the smallest stable radius a solid nucleus must reach to keep growing during solidification. It equals twice the interfacial energy times the melting temperature divided by the latent heat per volume times the undercooling, so larger undercooling yields a smaller critical radius.
notes: Valid for homogeneous nucleation; undercooling dT must be positive (below the melting point). Nuclei smaller than this radius tend to redissolve rather than grow.

name: Critical Free Energy of Nucleation
description: Computes the energy barrier that must be overcome to form a stable nucleus in homogeneous nucleation. It equals sixteen pi times the interfacial energy cubed divided by three times the volume free-energy change squared, representing the peak of the free-energy curve versus radius.
notes: Interfacial energy enters as the cube, so it dominates the barrier. dGv is the magnitude of the volume free-energy driving force; a larger driving force lowers the barrier sharply.

name: Avrami (JMAK) Transformed Fraction
description: Gives the fraction of material transformed after a given time during an isothermal phase transformation. It follows one minus the exponential of minus the rate constant times time raised to the Avrami exponent, producing the characteristic S-shaped transformation curve.
notes: Result is a dimensionless fraction between 0 and 1. The Avrami exponent na reflects nucleation and growth geometry; the rate constant ka must match the time units used.

name: Weibull Failure Probability
description: Gives the probability that a brittle specimen fails at or below a given applied stress. It equals one minus the exponential of minus the stress divided by the characteristic strength raised to the Weibull modulus, describing the statistical scatter of brittle fracture.
notes: Result is a probability between 0 and 1. A higher Weibull modulus mw means less scatter and a sharper failure threshold; s0 is the stress at which about 63 percent of specimens fail.

name: Orowan Stress (Precipitate Bypass)
description: Estimates the extra shear stress needed for a dislocation to bow around and bypass non-shearable precipitates. It equals the shear modulus times the Burgers vector divided by the particle spacing, so closely spaced particles give stronger hardening.
notes: Ls is the effective spacing between particles along the dislocation line; smaller spacing raises the stress. This simplified form omits logarithmic corrections used in refined Orowan models.

name: Taylor Hardening Flow Stress
description: Gives the flow stress contribution from stored dislocations via Taylor hardening. It equals a constant times the shear modulus times the Burgers vector times the square root of the dislocation density, so strength rises with the square root of dislocation density.
notes: This is the dislocation-hardening component only, not the total yield stress; add lattice friction and other terms separately. The constant alp typically ranges from about 0.2 to 0.5.

name: Elastic Modulus from Sound Velocity
description: Derives an effective elastic modulus from the longitudinal sound speed in a material. It equals the density times the square of the longitudinal wave speed, linking acoustic measurements to stiffness.
notes: This gives the longitudinal (P-wave) modulus, not Young's modulus; the two differ by Poisson's-ratio factors. Requires the longitudinal wave speed, not the shear or bulk wave speed.

name: Elastic Modulus of Porous Solid (Mackenzie)
description: Estimates how porosity lowers the elastic modulus of a solid using the Mackenzie relation. The modulus equals the fully dense value times one minus 1.9 times the porosity plus 0.9 times the porosity squared, so stiffness drops as pores are added.
notes: Porosity Pf is a fraction between 0 and 1, not a percentage. The empirical coefficients are calibrated for low-to-moderate porosity and lose accuracy at high pore fractions.

name: Curie-Weiss Susceptibility
description: Gives the magnetic susceptibility of a paramagnet above its Curie temperature. It equals the Curie constant divided by the difference between the temperature and the Curie temperature, so susceptibility diverges as the temperature approaches the Curie point.
notes: Valid only above the Curie temperature; T must exceed Tc or the result becomes negative or infinite. The law breaks down close to the transition where fluctuations dominate.

name: Nernst-Einstein Relation
description: Links ionic mobility to the diffusion coefficient via the Nernst-Einstein relation. The diffusion coefficient equals the mobility times the Boltzmann constant times temperature divided by the charge, connecting drift under a field to thermal diffusion.
notes: Uses charge per carrier (here the elementary charge); for multiply charged ions replace qe with the actual ion charge. Assumes dilute, non-interacting carriers and ideal behavior.

name: Characteristic Diffusion Time
description: Estimates the time scale for diffusion to spread over a given distance. It equals the diffusion distance squared divided by the diffusion coefficient, capturing the fact that diffusion time grows with the square of distance.
notes: This is an order-of-magnitude characteristic time, not an exact solution; a leading numerical factor of order one is omitted. Doubling the distance roughly quadruples the time.

name: Read-Shockley Grain Boundary Energy
description: Gives the energy of a low-angle grain boundary as a function of misorientation using the Read-Shockley model. It equals the energy coefficient times the angle times a core constant minus the natural log of the angle, rising steeply at small angles.
notes: Valid only for low-angle boundaries where the misorientation th is small (in radians); it does not apply to high-angle boundaries. The log term requires a positive angle.

name: Peierls-Nabarro Stress
description: Estimates the intrinsic lattice stress needed to move a dislocation through a perfect crystal. It equals the shear modulus times the exponential of minus two pi times the dislocation width divided by the Burgers vector, so wider dislocations move far more easily.
notes: Extremely sensitive to the width-to-Burgers-vector ratio because it sits in an exponential; small changes in wd shift the result by orders of magnitude. The estimate is model-dependent.

name: Thermal Expansion Mismatch Stress
description: Estimates the thermal stress that builds up between two bonded materials with different expansion coefficients. It equals Young's modulus times the CTE difference times the temperature change divided by one minus Poisson's ratio, as used for constrained films and coatings.
notes: The 1 minus Poisson's ratio term accounts for biaxial constraint typical of thin films on substrates. Result is a magnitude; a temperature drop puts a mismatched film into tension or compression depending on sign.
